extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology, literary theory, and advanced creative writers studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and classification of narrative pacing (tempo) in the novel: defines canonical narrative 'movements' (scene, summary, descriptive pause, ellipsis), their temporal formulas (relations of narrative time NT and story/diegetic time ST), and formal varieties (explicit/implicit, definite/indefinite, characterizing). Useful for analyzing or composing novelistic pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four canonical narrative movements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four basic forms of narrative movement (the 'four narrative movements'): ellipsis, descriptive pause (pause), scene, and summary. These govern narrative tempo in the novel and are treated as the canonical set historically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette treats these four as the restricted canonical forms; he observes no widely actualized canonical form symmetrical to summary (i.e., NT > ST 'slow-motion' scenes are not canonical). Examples and counterexamples from the tradition are discussed (Proust, Balzac, Fielding, Stendhal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene
rubrics_metrics.description: Scene conventionally realizes the equality of time between narrative and story: NT = ST.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most often realized in dialogue; scene preserves simultaneity of narrated duration and narrated events. Genette notes Proust's scenes are usually genuine scenes (including anachronies) rather than offhand glances; pure dialogue cannot be 'slowed down.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary
rubrics_metrics.description: A form with variable tempo that covers the range between scene and ellipsis (NT < ST in formulaic terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary can be brief paragraphs/pages that narrate several days/months/years without detailed action or speech; historically functions as the usual transition between scenes and the 'connective tissue' of the novel. Summary often serves retrospective sections (complete analepses) and can be used in both rapid transition and characterizing forms (e.g., 'some years of happiness').

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive pause (pause)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative sections that correspond to no duration in the story (NT > 0 while ST = 0): description as a pause in action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette distinguishes description-as-diegetic (part of the spatio-temporal universe of the story) from author's intrusions/commentarial excursuses (present-tense interventions). He emphasizes the concept of 'descriptive pause' (not every description is a pause) and warns against conflating descriptive pause with all description or with all pauses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description vs. author's intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions (diegetic) are constituents of the story's spatio-temporal universe and thus part of narrative discourse; commentarial excursuses in the present tense (author's intrusions) are not strictly narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't confuse descriptive passages (diegetic) with present-tense authorial interventions; both may occupy narrative space differently and have different effects on pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative narrative/iterative description
rubrics_metrics.description: Iterative narrative synthesizes recurring analogous moments into a single descriptive section (e.g., repeated appearances of a sight synthesized into one passage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iterative descriptions do not slow or pause narrative; they often accelerate or summarize multiple instances into one and are common in novels (Proust has many iterative descriptions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of 'slow-motion' canonical form (NT > ST)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no widely realized canonical form symmetrical to summary (i.e., a form where NT > ST, a scene deliberately slowed so that reading takes much longer than diegetic time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large or long scenes (e.g., some Proustian passages) are generally extended by extranarrative elements or interrupted by descriptive material rather than by genuine temporal slowing; experiments exist but are marginal rather than canonical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description absorbed into narration (Proust-specific claim)
rubrics_metrics.description: In Proust, clear descriptive passages are relatively few and usually do not produce a pause: description becomes absorbed into narration because Proust's 'description' typically narrates the perceptual activity of a character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette argues Proustian description is an active, intellectual, often physical contemplation by the character (perceptions, discoveries, corrections), so the descriptive piece narrates a 'whole story' and does not suspend story temporality; therefore 'descriptive pause' does not exist in Proust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis (temporal ellipsis) — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipsis is the omission of story time (NT = 0, ST = n): passage in which events are skipped over in story time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette treats ellipsis only in its temporal sense here and distinguishes it from paralipsis (lateral omissions). He notes ellipses can be definite (explicitly dated) or indefinite, and can be explicit or implicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit vs. implicit ellipses; definite vs. indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicit ellipses are announced in the text either by a temporal indication (definite or indefinite) or by pure elision followed by a later time indication; implicit ellipses are not announced and must be inferred from gaps in narrative continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit+indicated ellipses can function like quick summaries; the form with pure elision plus later indication is more rigorously elliptical. Implicit ellipses may remain uncharacterized and create opaque silences in the text (e.g., gaps around the grandmother's death in Proust).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterizing ellipses
rubrics_metrics.description: Ellipses can be 'characterizing' when the omission is accompanied by diegetic information (e.g., 'some years of happiness passed') that defines the omitted period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterizing ellipses are a standard novelistic resource (Genette gives examples from Stendhal, Fielding, and Proust). A negative characterization ('nothing worthy occurred') is equally a form of characterization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceleration vs. ellipsis
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceleration is narrative speeding that can approach or cross into ellipsis; the boundary between rapid summary/acceleration and outright ellipsis can be fuzzy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette observes that in some contexts (notably Proust's commentary on Balzac) a sudden change of tempo may be perceived as an ellipsis (a 'silence') rather than mere acceleration; analysts should be alert to when rapid narration effectively functions as omission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Descriptive intrusions by the narrator (present-tense asides)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brief present-tense descriptive intrusions by the narrator differ from diegetic description and can interrupt or comment upon narrative flow without being full descriptive pauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genette notes these are generally very brief and if present should be counted separately when analyzing narrative temporality and voice.
